ABSTRACT
The development of new energy technologies enables the construction of sustainable energy systems, and
deepens coupling between multi-energy resources and traditional energy-consuming objects, and complicates
data in the design process. Meanwhile, balancing low carbon requirements and economic needs should be further
optimized, and it posing a challenge for establishing an optimal energy system design method considering
technical, economic, and environmental triple requirements. To address this gap, this work firstly explores a
technology optimization approach for the energy supply and proposes a system holistic optimization model
including two steps. The first approach utilizes Generative Adversarial Networks(GAN) to address the demand
data deficiency. The second approach proposes an improved multi-objective Non-dominant Sorting Genetic
Algorithm-III(NSGA-III) model to solve the non-local optimal problem of balancing two objectives. Results
indicate that the proposed model achieves higher prediction efficiency than traditional methods, with an average
R
2
value 13.79 % better than a baseline neural network model. Furthermore, the whole-system design approach
proposed in this paper addresses the issue of different optimization ranges for various objectives, and reduces the
life cycle carbon emissions (LCCE) and life cycle cost(LCC) of the optimal scheme by 34.74 % and 20.69 %,
respectively, and the optimal emission is 54.78t. Multi-dimensional analysis indicates that the holistic optimi-
zation performs excellently, catering to present and future energy needs better.
1. Introduction
At present, the energy structure dominated by coal, oil and gas has
caused a global energy and environmental crisis. The current energy
consumption pattern is not sustainable for human society. It is impera-
tive to carry out energy conservation and emission reduction upgrades
across the entire energy system under net-zero targets, which is
conducive to meeting present and future green energy needs and
improving people ’ s living standards [1,2] .
The design phase presents the best opportunity for energy saving,
representing the most effective measure in the overall process of energy
system development . It is widely believed that the planning of multi-
energy systems is a critical stage that determines energy consumption
and carbon emissions performance throughout the whole system life
cycle. The rationality of this stage dominates the impact of subsequent
construction or operation activities on the environment and resource
consumption. As an important method of architectural design
evaluation, and a development branch of techno-economic assessments
(TEA) [3] , life cycle assessment (LCA) focuses on assessing the overall
situation of a building throughout its life cycle. In detail, minimum life
cycle carbon emissions(LCCE) and life cycle cost (LCC) are commonly
set as targets, which typically present a dual demand relationship
throughout the life cycle, encompassing products, processes, and ac-
tivities among other aspects [4,5] . LCCE focuses on evaluating carbon
dioxide emissions produced throughout their entire life cycle, including
all carbon equivalent emissions and outputs at different stages of the life
cycle. LCC is widely used to accurately determine total costs over a
specific period, and design cost usually increase with construction
progress [6] . At the same time, with the deepening of multi-energy
system research [7] , and the rapid development of material and en-
ergy flow interaction [8] , the research of combining information with
life cycle assessment has attracted extensive attention [9] . Therefore,
how to reasonably carry out the life cycle design of a building energy
system from a whole information physical fusion system perspective has

become a new scientific problem.
To address this issue, it is essential to clarify the input mode of data
processing based on energy demand prediction, and establish a
reasonable model to output multi-objective optimization results. Previ-
ous studies have primarily employed two methods for energy demand
setting: software modeling and data-driven approaches. Common
modeling software includes EnergyPlus, eQUEST and others. However,
modeling can be demanding and time-consuming. Data-driven algo-
rithms primarily utilize machine learning and other algorithms to make
predictions based on historical data. Shao et al. established an energy
consumption prediction model for hotels using a support vector machine
with HVAC and weather data as input parameters [10] . Tian et al.
proposed a novel energy consumption predictive model called FCM-
GWO-BP neural network to address the unclear physical significance,
poor data generalization, and low fitting accuracy issues of the con-
ventional backpropagation neural network model [11] . Rocio et al.
identified influencing parameters including personnel density, building
geometry, and natural ventilation volume [12] . Zhang et al. adopted the
Clustering Decision Tree algorithm to address the issue of data imbal-
ance and identify building operating conditions [13] . In essence, tradi-
tional methods primarily rely on model building and existing historical
data. To achieve good performance, the training dataset must be
representative and contain sufficient diversity. However, collecting such
representative and extensive data is challenging, costly, and time-
consuming [14] , especially in new buildings and energy-efficient ret-
rofitted buildings. If we lack sufficient data or if the sampled data de-
viates from the true data distribution, it can impact prediction accuracy.
Recent years, to overcome these problems, and enhance the learning
ability of machine learning methods, and improve the quality of artifi-
cial data, and increase the prediction accuracy, researchers have turned
their attention to Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), which
can generate high-quality training samples to supplement and extend
real data. GAN is a cutting-edge topic in deep learning and artificial
intelligence, and capable of exploring complex data distributions and
generating high-quality samples that effectively supplement real data
[15] . The GAN model was first proposed by Goodfellow et al in 2014
[16] . Different from traditional adversarial models, GANs do not directly
estimate the probability density of each sample point in the sample
space, but instead implicitly express the distribution of the generator to
the sample through the adversarial process [17] . GAN comprehensively
considers numerous factors, such as changing trends and data correla-
tions. Douzas et al. utilized GAN to approximate the real data distribu-
tion and generate data for several imbalanced datasets [18] . Literature
[19] have respectively applied GAN to realize data enhancement for
imbalanced data, image and sequence data to improve accuracy pre-
diction. Esteban et al. proposed a recursive GAN and a recursive con-
ditional GAN to generate realistic multi-dimensional medical time series
[20] . Tang et al. proposed a method for programmatic data enhance-
ment using an auxiliary classifier GAN [21] . Compared with datasets in
research fields such as image recognition and speech processing, the
number of datasets in building energy carbon emission and cost time
series is relatively small, and there is still a lack of datasets in the field of
new construction. GAN provides an effective tool for enhancing data
generation and predicting building characteristics. The proposed
method, which does not rely on historical data, instead making pre-
dictions based on key features has the potential to significantly
contribute to research on sustainable energy system design.
Furthermore, multi-objective optimization algorithms have been
widely used in architectural design optimization [22 – 24] . However,
most genetic algorithm-based multi-objective optimization algorithms
adopt simple and fixed evolutionary strategies, which are not ideal for
complex applications such as architectural design optimization. The
Non-dominant Sorting Genetic Algorithm-II (NSGA-II), developed in
2002, is capable of exploring the optimal solution for fast sorting se-
lection. It maintains the optimal individual from parents in the offspring
and generates a set of non-dominant Pareto optimal solutions, thereby
significantly improving optimization efficiency [25] . The Non-dominant
Sorting Genetic Algorithm-III (NSGA-III) is an update to the NSGA-II
algorithm, utilizing a reference point mechanism to emphasize non-
dominant group members and enhance the robustness and effective-
ness of the results [26] . Chen et al. compared the optimization perfor-
mance of NSGA-II, NSGA-III and the multi-objective evolutionary
algorithm based on decomposition to determine the best building per-
formance, and indicated that NSGA-III has the highest optimization ef-
ficiency [27] . As reported in reference [28] , Zhai et al. combined the
non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm(NSGA-II) with Energy Plus to

optimize the glass characteristics and select a design plan that balanced
building energy performance. However, the aforementioned algorithm
faces challenges in intensifying selection pressure on the Pareto optimal
frontier and obtaining well-diversified solution sets under different
optimization ranges of different objectives. Furthermore, the algo-
rithm ’ s accuracy and calculation speed should be improved.
Despite prior research, in the field of energy system optimization,
under economic and carbon emission dual requirements, there remains a
lack of efficient, convincing design methods for data deficient energy
system lifetime designs. Therefore, the research takes LCCE and LCC as
important optimization targets and aims to obtain a suitable design
method. The proposed method of multi improved NSGA-III optimization
algorithm was proposed. Analysis of total cost, renewable energy utili-
zation, carbon emissions, and other indicators in the design stage can
effectively guide the building and energy system towards uniform
standards. This approach aids in determining different energy system
design schemes and related parameters in a more scientific and
reasonable manner.
The study integrated the energy system and building organically as a
whole. The calculation and analysis of carbon emissions in the design
stage can optimize system configuration and energy parameters. The
energy system plan can be obtained throughout the entire life cycle via a
mixed design scheme. The first part of this paper outlines the research
content and the subsequent parts presenting the following: The second
part primarily introduces the holistic system approach boundary to
building integrated energy systems, covering model architecture, design
data sources, model establishment, optimization algorithms and
constraint conditions; The third part conducts a case study of an office
building in Shaanxi Province, and mainly introducing feature screening,
optimal design results, optimal emission reduction outputs, and other
topics; The fourth part analyzes the paradigmatic method and conducts
concrete data analysis to propose an alternative optimization scheme;
Finally, we summarize the contents of the article. Fig. 1 depicts the
process and steps of this study.
2. The whole-system of building integrated energy system
2.1. Model architecture
This study aims to investigate integrated building energy system
design across the whole-system and full life cycle, and proposes an
improved multi-objective NSGA-III optimization algorithm under the
whole system structure. At the physical level, the carbon emissions of
the system are calculated and the main characteristics extracted. At the
data level, the migration algorithm is used to train the model, yielding a
high-precision model for predicting life cycle carbon emissions (LCCE)
and life cycle cost (LCC). The model architecture is depicted in the figure
below, and the options for energy systems including power grids, solar
photovoltaic panels, cooling water storage units, hot water storage units
and other low carbon energy technologies. The proposed method can
effectively predict and optimize LCCE and LCC, thereby obtaining the
optimal design scheme. In this study, we verify its effectiveness from the
perspective of the whole life cycle performance of buildings, and add
new sampling methods, algorithms and optimization algorithms to
enrich its content. We propose a new method for selecting the optimal
building and integrated system scheme, making the strategy more
rigorous and practical. Fig. 2 depicts the whole-system holistic optimi-
zation approach. This research ’ s originality comprises the following
three elements:

consistent, user-friendly, and accurate. This study quantitatively
assessed life cycle carbon emissions (LCCE) in accordance with China ’ s
National Building Carbon Emission Standard (GBT 51366 – 2019) [29] .

Measurement of building system boundaries and carbon emissions is
a key part of life cycle assessment (LCA). The LCA, as defined by ISO
14040, is the process of preparing and assessing the input, output and
potential environmental impact of a product system throughout its life
cycle. Before carbon emissions prediction, the study defines the target
system boundaries, including building space boundaries and life cycle
process boundaries. Fig. 2 illustrates the scope boundary, which corre-
sponds to the scope of the study. It encompasses both the building body
and the energy supply system. The building life cycle is divided into five
main stages, referred to as clade to gate , with details available in Fig. 3 .
These stages are: material production, transportation, construction,
operation and maintenance, and demolition . The objective of the study
is to develop an integrated energy system sustainability design that ac-
counts for life-cycle carbon emissions and costs. Furthermore, the
building life cycle inventory data is imported into the corresponding
engineering software, Glodon.

The uncertainty of buildings carbon emissions is greatly affected by

requirement.

2.3. Basic data acquisition
Primary data can be obtained by reviewing design drawings, pur-
chase lists and other engineering construction related technical data. It
is straightforward to ascertain the consumption of various building
materials required for construction projects through the bill of quanti-
ties, the bill of materials and so on.
During project exploration, the geological exploration rig consumes
energy. However, considering its short working time and low energy
consumption, the calculation time boundary for carbon emission in the
construction stage is stipulated to start from the tool ’ s arrival on site.
In the production of building materials, if low-value waste is used as
a raw material, the carbon footprint of its upstream process can be
overlooked. If other recycled materials are used, they should be calcu-
lated as 50 % of the carbon emissions of the primary materials they
replace. Renewable construction waste generated during the construc-
tion and demolition phases of a building, accounts for 50 % of the carbon
emissions associated with primary materials. This waste should be
properly managed and replaced with more sustainable alternatives, in
Y. Tian and K. Chai

7
order to reduce the overall carbon footprint of the building.
During building construction, the energy power required for the
operation of construction machinery and small equipment is a major
source of carbon emissions. Normal respiration and carbon dioxide
release are normal physiological processes for humans, and there is no
significant difference in the amount of carbon dioxide breathed and
released by construction workers compared to the general population, so
it is not included in the carbon emissions of construction workers. Ma-
terials, components and parts used in construction, such as ready-mixed
concrete, concrete components, precast piles, doors and windows, are
typically produced off-site and therefore excluded from energy con-
sumption during the construction phase. The energy consumption of
materials, components and parts mixed and produced on-site should be
included. To facilitate the turnover of the structure, the construction
phase typically utilizes sandwich color steel plate for temporary struc-
tures, such as movable boards, houses and container houses. These
simple temporary houses are easy to install and dismantle, requiring
little energy for construction and dismantlement, and are not included in
carbon emissions calculations during the building ’ s construction phase.

2.5. Prediction and evaluation
2.5.1. Prediction model
GAN proposed by Ian Goodfellow et al. in 2014, and published in the
paper Generative Adversarial Networks , which is mainly inspired by
the zero-sum game idea in game theory. As shown in Fig. 5 , in deep
learning neural networks, G (Generator) and D (Discriminator) are in a
constant game-like interaction where they attempt to outsmart each
other in order for G to learn the distribution of the data. The relationship
is as follows: the discriminator punishes the generator, benefiting itself
while the generator loses. The generator evolves such that the discrim-
inator punishes itself less, benefiting the generator and causing the
discriminator to lose. In the GAN framework, the generator and
discriminator models engage in continuous training game with each
other, aiming to bring the generator samples closer to the real data
distribution, and improve the discriminator ’ s ability to distinguish be-
tween generator samples and real data. During training, the goal of the
generator is to deceive the discriminator, while the goal of the
discriminator is to distinguish between samples generated by the
generator and real data. Random search and grid search methods are
used to select appropriate hyperparameters in the neural network to
realize the operation of the prediction model [36] .
In detail, G is a generative network that receives random noise. D is a
discriminant network that determines whether a given set of data is real;
its input parameter is x. The output D(X) represents the probability that
X is the real data. The output of 1 indicates that the data is 100 %
genuine, while an output of 0 suggests that it is impossible for the data to
be authentic. The algorithm steps are as follows:

2.6. Multi-objective optimization
The constructed multi-objective model has different physical mean-
ings for the objects and a large difference in orders of magnitude, which
requires careful consideration. Considering the sequential characteris-
tics of the system, this study adopted the normalization distance be-
tween the objective function values of each group of non-inferior
solutions in the Pareto frontier and the ideal point as the evaluation
index. Then, select a group of non-inferior solutions closest to the ideal
point as the best operation scheme. Here, the ideal point refers to the
point on the Pareto frontier that minimizes the objective function, which
is the origin of the coordinate axis after normalization. The distance
refers to the spatial distance between two points in the DeKale coordi-
nate system. Based on NSGA-III [39] , a double-improved algorithm
named AHA-VaEA-NSGA-III was proposed to further enhance the
robustness and speed of the model. To ensure convergence of the solu-
tion set, the model selects the solution with best convergence as the non-
dominant solution in the same small scale. To maintain diversity in the
solution set, in any two different small territories, the solution with good
convergence and distribution in one small territory dominates the so-
lution with poor convergence and distribution in the other small terri-
tory. The proposed domination relation is embedded in VaEA to replace
the Pareto domination relation. To reduce computational burden and
improve model accuracy, the Artificial Hummingbird Algorithm (AHA)
is utilized to optimize the model. Fig. 6 depicts an algorithm consisting
of three stages, whose details are described as follows.
The first stage is the Artificial Hummingbird Algorithm.

Step 1.2. Hummingbirds constantly seek out better food sources and
exhibit superior adaptation values.

the territorial bird, while the rest are considered follower birds. Next,
when there is no approaching bird from the territorial bird, the heuristic

4. Analysis and verification
To verify the feasibility of the model under different energy forms,
the study takes different sustainable energy system plan schemes as
examples. The analysis further examines the investment cost, operation
and maintenance cost, equipment salvage value, and total cost under
different investment plans. This study compares five schemes.
• Scheme 1: the traditional electric cooling and heating mode, which
comprises the power grid, electric boiler, and water chilling unit.
• Scheme 2: the conventional electric cooling and heating mode, as
well as photovoltaic generation.
• Scheme 3: traditional electric cooling and heating mode, and
photovoltaic generation, and energy storage.
• Scheme 4: traditional electric cooling and heating mode, and
photovoltaic generation, and energy storage, and pump.
• Scheme 5: traditional electric cooling and heating mode, and
photovoltaic generation, and energy storage, and pump, and
hydrogen.
To obtain multi-objective optimization results, the optimal solution
should be derived from the Pareto optimal solution set. This dataset
comprises decision variable solutions that satisfy the Pareto optimal
state. Because the optimization objectives are contradictory, the results
of each multi-objective algorithm are expected to show a convergence
trend. The traditional scheme is often to explore the best spot from the
Pareto frontier [44] . Once the ideal point is determined, the distance
between each optimal point in the Pareto front set and the ideal point is
calculated. However, because of the different ranges of changes for each
target, some targets with large changes will affect site selection and the
final scheme. This study adopts the multi improved NSGA-III method, as
described above, for scheme selection to reduce the influence of
different variation ranges on scheme selection. Technoeconomic as-

5. Conclusion
This study proposes a new strategy that integrates building and en-
ergy systems to obtain the system design scheme from a whole-system
full life cycle perspective. The results prove that this strategy is an
effective method to balance LCCE and LCC, and makes the optimization
results of each objective more reasonable, outperforming traditional
methods. The main conclusions of this study are as follows:
